solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Superman’s girl is about to drop Italian dish

indicators.note: to be about something is to stand around it, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: Lois Lane is Superman's girlfriend in the comics
to sag is to droop or drop

explanation.surface: Lois Lane is about to let an Italian dish fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is about to drop' reads as a single threat of falling; split it, and 'is about' is the holding signal while 'to drop' is a verb in its own right.
explanation.definitionFit: Lasagne is a baked pasta dish from Italy, layered with sauce and cheese.

clue.text: Green gunk, skimmed

indicators.note: skimming takes off the top layer, so the first letter is removed

blocks.note: slime is sticky gunk

explanation.surface: Green scum is being skimmed off the surface of a pond.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the top is the first letter, so skimming SLIME loses its S.
explanation.definitionFit: Lime is a bright yellowish shade of the colour, named after the citrus fruit.

clue.text: Having had a few seconds, one brushed up on geometry in the end

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that letter is kept

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for seconds
a quiff is hair brushed up and back from the forehead
final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone who has had a few seconds to spare revises geometry at the last moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A few seconds' looks like a phrase about time, but the definition is 'Having had a few', meaning drinks. Squiffy is British slang for slightly drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has had a few drinks is tipsy, and squiffy is a colloquial word for that tipsy state.

clue.text: Entire amount, repellent

blocks.note: first meaning: the total before deductions
second meaning: disgusting

explanation.walkthrough: Two unrelated senses of one word sit side by side, separated only by the comma.
explanation.definitionFit: Gross pay is the whole sum before tax, and something gross is disgusting or revolting.

clue.text: Flag yours truly raised, with America retaining title

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising something lifts it upwards so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: to flag is to tire or weaken
the setter refers to themself
abbreviation for the United States

explanation.surface: Someone raises their own flag, with America keeping hold of a title.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag' looks like a banner but is the verb meaning to tire. 'Retaining' looks like a container signal but belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An emeritus professor keeps the honorary rank after retiring from the post.

clue.text: Rubbish plant used as dessert

blocks.note: first meaning: nonsense, empty talk
second meaning: the pink-stalked vegetable stewed in puddings

explanation.surface: A worthless weed has been served up as pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: Rhubarb is British slang for nonsense, from actors muttering the word to make background chatter.
explanation.definitionFit: The plant's sour stalks are cooked with sugar in crumbles and pies, and the word also means nonsense talk.

clue.text: Male feeding horses in book

indicators.note: food fed to an animal goes inside it, so one piece is put within another

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for male
roans are horses with a mixed-coloured coat

explanation.surface: A man feeding horses appears in a book.
explanation.walkthrough: The book is a biblical one: Paul's Epistle to the Romans in the New Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: Romans is one of the New Testament books, a letter written by Saint Paul.

clue.text: Fun unfortunately suffering for sure

indicators.note: something that has gone unfortunately has gone wrong, so the letters come out in a wrong order

blocks.note: taken as written
ailing means ill or suffering

explanation.surface: Having fun, unfortunately, means certain suffering later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfortunately' reads as a comment on the fun, but it only rearranges three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unfailing never lets you down, so it can be relied upon with complete certainty.

clue.text: Way to stuff a European champion

indicators.note: stuffing fills something, so one piece is packed inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
a Pole is a person from Poland
ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A route found to fill a European champion with food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Champion' suggests a sports winner, but here it means someone who promotes a cause.
explanation.definitionFit: An apostle is a passionate advocate for an idea, just as a champion supports and promotes a cause.

clue.text: American man crushing queen like a snake

indicators.note: crushing something holds it tightly in a grip, so one piece clasps others

blocks.note: buster is an American way of addressing a man
HM is Her Majesty
as means in the manner of, like

explanation.surface: An American man crushes a queen as a snake would.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like a snake' seems to describe the crushing, but 'like' supplies AS and 'a snake' is the definition. BUSH tempts as the American; it leaves nothing workable.
explanation.definitionFit: The bushmaster is a large venomous pit viper found in Central and South America.

clue.text: Large tomb, parent bagging a posh one

indicators.note: to bag something is to put it into a bag, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: mum is mother
taken as written
U means upper-class
sole means only, single

explanation.surface: A parent secures a grand tomb for one well-to-do person.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class is a crossword convention from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A mausoleum is a large stately building housing a burial chamber, named after King Mausolus.

clue.text: Fine no longer having clean teeth

blocks.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
loss is the state of no longer having something

explanation.surface: Someone is no longer in good shape because they skipped brushing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No longer having' looks like a deletion signal, but it is a definition of a noun in its own right.
explanation.definitionFit: To floss is to clean between the teeth with a waxed thread.

clue.text: Mink possibly, clothing slave?

blocks.note: first meaning: an animal killed so its fur can be worn, sacrificed to style
second meaning: a person in thrall to whatever is currently being worn

explanation.surface: A mink is killed so its pelt can clothe someone in thrall to trends.
explanation.walkthrough: The mink is literally sacrificed for clothes, while the person is only figuratively enslaved to them; the question mark flags the animal as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes someone who follows every trend slavishly, and also a creature literally killed for its pelt.

clue.text: Flexible parts to deliver, chattering away

indicators.note: something that parts is split open, letting another piece sit in the gap

blocks.note: lithe means supple, flexible
to bring is to deliver

explanation.surface: Supple parts are to be delivered while someone chatters on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parts' looks like a plural noun, but it is a verb: the flexible word splits the delivering word apart.
explanation.definitionFit: To blither is to talk nonsense at length, so blithering is rambling, incessant chatter.

clue.text: Ne’er-do-well has to settle a fight

blocks.note: to lay is to set down or settle
taken as written
a bout is a boxing match

explanation.surface: A good-for-nothing is obliged to end a scrap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settle a fight' reads as making peace; instead the words are taken separately, as laying down and a boxing contest.
explanation.definitionFit: A layabout is an idle, lazy person who avoids work, much like a good-for-nothing.

clue.text: Wind light — it’s a scorcher?

blocks.note: wind blows
a torch gives light

explanation.surface: A light breeze arrives on a very hot day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind light' looks like a weather forecast, and 'scorcher' suggests a hot day; the tool is what scorches.
explanation.definitionFit: A blowtorch produces an intense flame for burning off paint, so it scorches whatever it touches.

clue.text: Several loons?

definitions.note: plural noun, as is the answer

blocks.note: first meaning: an old word for various, sundry
second meaning: water birds that plunge under the surface

explanation.surface: A handful of crazy people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loons' suggests lunatics, but it is the North American name for the birds British birders call divers.
explanation.definitionFit: Divers is an archaic adjective for sundry, and it is also the British name for the diving water birds.

clue.text: Lean man, legal official

blocks.note: to tip is to lean over
to man a post is to staff it

explanation.surface: A thin man works as an officer of the court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lean' and 'man' read as adjective and noun, but both are verbs.
explanation.definitionFit: A tipstaff is a court officer, originally carrying a metal-tipped staff, who enforces orders of arrest.

clue.text: Excellent advice corporation rejected

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so it reads the other way

blocks.note: a tip is a piece of advice
corporation is jocular slang for a pot belly

explanation.surface: A company turned down some first-rate advice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' seems to mean a company, but it is old slang for a large paunch, and so for pot.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiptop is a colloquial word for first-class or of the highest quality.

clue.text: Fast approaching northern English city

blocks.note: presto is the musical term for very fast
N is the abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: Speeding towards a city in the north of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Northern' seems to describe the city but gives only its letter. Preston is a city in Lancashire, north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Preston is the administrative centre of Lancashire and was granted city status in 2002.

clue.text: I issued new clasps good for mask

indicators.note: something new is made afresh, so the letters are put into a fresh order
to clasp is to hold in a grip, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: taken as written
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Someone hands out new clasps, good ones for a mask.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New clasps' reads as fresh fasteners; 'new' signals the rearrangement and 'clasps' the holding.
explanation.definitionFit: A disguise hides who you are, just as a mask conceals the face.

clue.text: Trying exotic Eskimo rolls, initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept
something exotic is strange and foreign, so the letters appear in an unfamiliar order

blocks.note: taken as written
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Attempting fancy kayak rolls, at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: An Eskimo roll is a kayaking manoeuvre, which makes 'Trying' look like attempting rather than annoying.
explanation.definitionFit: Something trying tests your patience, and irksome means annoying or tiresome in the same way.

clue.text: Chinese food that’s totally stupid?

blocks.note: dim means slow-witted
a sum is a total

explanation.surface: A Chinese meal that is utterly foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words are read backwards against the clue: stupid in total, a dim sum.
explanation.definitionFit: Dim sum are small Cantonese dishes such as dumplings, usually served in bamboo steamers.

clue.text: Silly Eccles thick, or a serious jerk?

indicators.note: something silly is nonsensical, so these letters are jumbled into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A foolish, dim person from Eccles, or just a real idiot?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerk' looks like an insult to match 'thick', but it means a sudden spasm. Eccles is a town near Manchester.
explanation.definitionFit: A current passing through the body makes the muscles twitch violently, a serious involuntary spasm.

clue.text: Heart of stone, a shade open

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central part, so only the middle letter is kept

blocks.note: middle letter of the word
vert is green in heraldry

explanation.surface: A stone-hearted person is slightly more open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A shade open' reads as slightly open, but 'a shade' is a colour and 'open' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Overt means done openly and not concealed, the opposite of covert.

clue.text: Slip, small, on child

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
a kid is a child

explanation.surface: A small slip of clothing is put on a child.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue one piece placed on another sits above it.
explanation.definitionFit: A skid is an uncontrolled slide, as when a wheel slips on ice.

clue.text: Head of playwright missing, commit to the ground

indicators.note: the head is the first letter, and here it is said to be missing
something missing is absent, so that letter is dropped

blocks.note: Harold Pinter was an English playwright

explanation.surface: A headless playwright is being buried.
explanation.walkthrough: The dramatist is Harold Pinter, author of The Birthday Party and The Caretaker.
explanation.definitionFit: To inter is to bury a body, placing it in a grave in the earth.

clue.text: Labouring we do in the beginning?

definitions.text: Labouring we do in the beginning?

blocks.note: surface reading: hard manual toil such as digging
setter's reading: the dull preparatory effort done before the main task

explanation.surface: The hard graft we put in at the start of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the literal digging sense and the preparation sense are both meant.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the groundwork laid before a project, originally the digging done with a garden tool.

clue.text: Material that’s checked poorly leaving Medway town

indicators.note: to leave is to depart, so those letters go out of the word

blocks.note: Gillingham is a town on the River Medway in Kent
poorly means unwell, ill

explanation.surface: Fabric that has been checked badly on its way out of a Kent town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Checked poorly' reads as a sloppy inspection, but 'checked' belongs to the definition and 'poorly' supplies the removed letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Gingham is a cotton fabric woven in a pattern of small squares, typically white with a colour.

clue.text: Idiot with fanciful idea penning articles

indicators.note: to pen is to shut in an enclosure, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: a fad is a passing craze
THE and A are the definite and indefinite articles

explanation.surface: A fool with a whimsical notion is writing newspaper pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penning articles' suggests writing for a paper; here 'penning' means enclosing and the articles are grammatical words.
explanation.definitionFit: Fathead is an informal insult for a stupid person, a synonym of dolt or dimwit.
